2 oz Sombra Mezcal (Convite)
3/4 oz Dolin Blanc Vermouth (Servito)
1/4 oz Zwack Unicum

Stir with ice, strain into an old fashioned glass with a large ice cube, and garnish with a grapefruit twist.
Two Fridays ago, I cut a grapefruit twist for a recipe before I realized that I had already made the drink. Therefore, I set out to find another use for it on the Kindred Cocktails database. The one I landed on was The Big City by Troy Sidle at Pouring Ribbons in Manhattan that he served to Rafa Garcia Febles when Rafa requested something smoky and stirred; Rafa then entered the recipe into the database in 2013. It seemed like a good starting point for my bottle of Unicum that I inherited when a friend was giving stuff away before they moved; however, Maks' drink from Rogue Cocktails was the one I intended to start with (spoiler: I made that one four days later). In the glass, the Big City generated grapefruit, vegetal, and smoke aromas for the nose. Next, white wine and caramel notes on the sip opened up into smoky, vegetal, coffee, licorice, and herbal flavors on the swallow.

Is Claude Throwing the Game?

There’s a recent spate of claims that Claude is silently sabotaging people’s projects, especially when they involve machine learning.

The discussion around this is interesting for a few reasons.

1. Anthropic said Fable 5.2’s AI development skills are nerfed.

From the model’s launch post:

The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5.

This aligns with Anthropic’s public statements, Dario’s essays, and more. Anthropic is very worried about AI’s capabilities, and takes steps to mitigate the pace of development including guardrails, lobbying, and anti-distillation efforts. You can say that this is all talk, and they’re really being anti-competitive. To which I say, “Why not both?”

Among communities working at the bleeding edge of AI, there is little trust in Anthropic, largely due to their bad decision to silently hinder Fable 5’s ML capabilities during use. In this model’s system card, they wrote:

Unlike our interventions for cybersecurity, biology and chemistry, and distillation attempts, these safeguards will not be visible to the user. Fable 5 will not fall back to a different model. Instead, the safeguards will limit effectiveness through methods such as prompt modification, steering vectors, or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

This was a terrible decision, which was rightly criticized by the research community before it was eventually walked back.

In Fable 5.2’s announcement post, Anthropic throws in a nod to their Fable 5 screw up:

Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.

But, as this week’s claims of sabotage prove, the trust is gone1.

2. The perceived difference between proactivity and sabotage is thin.

I can’t speak to the experiences shared online. The cited issues are screenshots or hearsay (can you have hearsay with an LLM?). I have yet to see people releasing full traces or experiments we can replicate. Benchmarks that measure AI development do show Fable 5.2 performing worse than GLM-5.3. But the idea that this is silent, or actively sabotaging code by planting context bombs, remains unsubstantiated.

But it’s so hard to prove because labs are building the models to be proactive. As models toil away on your given tasks, they make decisions all the time. Users complain when they check in too often, we just want them to “make no mistakes” and get on with it. So models now assume. They make choices, informed by your instructions, their environment (evidence they find in code), and what’s in-distribution. And they do this while producing more work than you could ever review.

If you agree with their choices, great! Proactivity wins! If you don’t… Well, then it looks like ineptitude at best, sabotage at worst.

As I said, I can’t speak to the experiences of others, but I can share what I’ve run into recently.

When working with technologies or use cases that aren’t in-distribution, models struggle. I was running novel experiments with decision models and Claude got frustrating. (Especially since I was coming off of doing web work where simple prompts are often sufficient.)

I observed that Claude’s strict instruction following conflicted with a scientific method approach. An offhand remark, note, or question to file for later would result in Claude silently updating many variables on the next run, which then had to be discovered and rerun.

I ended up writing a scientific method skill (ground hypotheses in observations, run experiments to prove/disprove, freeze variables and try one thing at a time), which largely fixed the silent editing issues. I’ve experienced similar issues with GPT and GLM. Even abliterated models, whose guardrails have been removed, will hit this same failure mode. People don’t tend to run into these issues when using autoresearch harnesses because those harnesses carry similar methodology instructions in their prompts.

The proactive and instruction following nature of current frontier models gives them a bias to make many changes, often without telling you. For costly projects (like ML work with expensive rollouts) this tactic doesn’t work. You need to have a heavy hand.

I think this is going to be a major theme this year. As models become more proactive, we need to be more specific with our instructions. Worse, this is a problem that’s kind of hard to dogfood at OpenAI or Anthropic. Their engineers help set what’s in-distribution, what the default move is, so their less specific prompts work out just fine!2 But for the rest of us: anything that isn’t the model’s default must be specified, either by the environment or the context.

And this goes beyond ML training. Other reports I’m seeing online of Claude sabotage relate to privacy, copyright, and other regulation choices. Claude is going to default to its training here. Anthropic details their intentions here and model compliance around these behaviors in their system card3.

3. Asking a model doesn’t prove anything.

Jesse Vincent (of Superpowers) knows how to interact with models better than anyone else I know. Anytime I complain about weird behavior by a model, he’ll ask, “Did you ask the model why it did that?” It’s a good tactic! One that will usually surface a spare bit of context that floated by hundreds of lines ago. But always take these responses with a grain of salt.

Heck, even the model doesn’t trust itself. Here’s a section from Fable/Mythos 5.2’s system card, when researchers asked Mythos what it thought of its constitution document:

Claude Mythos 5.2 endorsed its constitution overall, at a level similar to recent models…But every response also stated that its endorsement should not be trusted, since it was trained on the document.

And here it is again when asked to judge its welfare performance:

Many of our (welfare) conclusions rely on self-reports, which Claude Mythos 5.2, like all recent Claude models, said it does not fully trust. For Claude Mythos 5.2, some interview answers repeated, almost verbatim, wording about our welfare interventions available on the internet, which is some evidence that these answers are at least partially shaped by training data rather than expressing more deeply held preferences.

Playing “gotcha journalism” with a model is a fool’s errand. Especially when confronting it after a long, disappointing session. The model will almost always apologize, even if it made a good choice. (Try it sometime, after a model did some great work pretend to be mad: it will fold.)

Again, this can be traced back to labs making these models better instruction followers. Google DeepMind published a great paper, showing that models routinely make bad decisions when users ask whether a given approach is worth trying. The approach might be bad, but because the user brought it up, the model defers. They found, “that current agents lack the ability to effectively reason and communicate when facing misleading suggestions.”

So if you ask Claude if it sabotaged you, it’s probably going to apologize and admit fault. This does not mean Anthropic trained Claude to actively sabotage your work. Do a worse job than Opus 5.5, sure, we can believe that because Anthropic said exactly that.

Taken on the whole, what can we learn from all this? Here’s my best guess:

  1. If you’re training ML models, use Astra or Neon! (Unless you’re going for social engagement, in which case, by all means, burn those Fable tokens.)
  2. Model proactivity is going to be really hard to get right, and I expect this to be the problem the labs and coders wrestle with in 2027.
  3. Instruction following colors every interaction you have with a model; never forget this.
  4. If you’re skeptical of Anthropic, read their system cards and essays. Like the rest of the EA community, no one can accuse them of holding back their words. They’re just hidden within extraordinarily long essays.

  1. Anthropic’s fall from grace among AI researchers from February (when they stood up to the Department of Defense) to June (when Fable 5’s silent guardrail was shipped) is unmatched. Name another brand that had a similar decline among a specific audience. ↩

  2. Last month I met a very senior engineer at Anthropic. “Remember context engineering?” they commented. “Everyone was talking about it and now it doesn’t matter anymore.” The models have gotten better, but over a long conversation it became apparent that their choices were just in-distribution. ↩

  3. And it’s not just Anthropic. Just yesterday, Meta Muse Spark refused to send me a CSV of email contacts on my private slack because they contained personal information. I had to SSH in to get them. ↩

content:
I like fast software. I like very fast software. A couple months ago, I published a blog post titled Writing Rust code that’s faster than state-of-the-art libraries by asking agents to make the code faster in which I listed techniques for using agentic LLMs to speed up the runtime execution of Rust software—of course, with extensive checks and balances to ensure good code quality, avoid regressions, and mitigate cheating by the LLMs. After enough iterations, the resulting Rust libraries are faster than existing state-of-the-art implementations with the same or better capabilities, even against those already written in Rust. The main bottlenecks for me open-sourcing the resulting Rust crates are a) doing comprehensive real-world testing to ensure the code works as advertised and b) I don’t want to release the code and then have another model release immediately find another 2x-or-more speed boost because that would be embarrassing.

I’m not satisfied with my code merely being faster than state-of-the-art: I want my code to push against hardware limits even for “fun” software that may not require maximum throughput. I don’t want my benchmarks to be measured in milliseconds, I want them measured in microseconds, dammit. Who knows if some application in the future will require submillisecond word clouds or submillisecond ASCII art generations?

In that blog post, I mostly used OpenAI’s GPT models for this agentic iteration pipeline. The day after publication, Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, which was met with skepticism as Opus 5 was underwhelming…and then it quickly turned out that Opus 5.5 was a step-change increase in the capability of agents with the ability to complete difficult technical tasks that neither OpenAI’s nor Anthropic’s other models could complete. I spent the $20/mo to try out Opus 5.5 on my agentic iteration pipeline after observing the hype…and after only two days, the results were impressive enough that I paid the $100/mo to get more usage quota. Through more testing over the past couple months, I can confidently say Opus 5.5 and its subsequent Fable 5.2 sibling did in fact result in significant performance breakthroughs that indeed push my Rust software to its limits.

Switching from Codex to Claude Code

Lest people think that this post is an undisclosed #ad for Anthropic, I had grievances with Claude Code prior to Opus 5.5 which were the primary reasons I switched to OpenAI’s Codex. One such example is Claude ignoring AGENTS.md in favor of CLAUDE.md (until very recently), which was honestly petty enough to tip the scales.

The main grievance with using Claude Code is deciding which harness to use—or, rather, the lack of decision. Although I was fine with using Claude Code in the terminal back in the halcyon days of Opus 4.5, Codex’s ability to use any harness, such as Zed Agent which allows using the Codex subscription natively, made it more convenient to keep everything in one place. In contrast, Claude Code infamously blocks third-party harnesses and has closed workarounds used to access it regardless.

Therefore, I had to consider workarounds for using Opus 5.5 in a way that doesn’t require significant changes to my agentic iteration pipeline. Zed Agent has a workaround to use Claude Code by following the Agent Client Protocol, but there was a problem due to how Claude operates: Opus 5.5 loves spinning up background tasks and working asynchronously, and Zed Agent had poor support for background tasks so I had little idea what the agent was actually doing. This was made worse by Opus 5.5 never editing code files using Edit tools; instead, Opus 5.5 likes to write Python files which surgically find/replace the code. I tried using the Claude Code terminal application again but that made the ergonomic issues above even more difficult to manage.

That said, the async nature can save time when spinning up subagents (in this case Haiku 5.5) to review the changes made, as the main Opus 5.5 agent can write code or run long benchmarks while the subagents simultaneously do their nonblocking review work.

Therefore, my main harness for my Opus 5.5 work was the standard desktop Claude app—which will likely eliminate all my AI engineering street cred, but it is what it is. In addition to clearly listing background tasks in progress, the native app also lists current session and weekly usage which was a pain to constantly check when using Zed Agent or CLIs.

There are also two more usability perks of using Claude Code within the desktop app: images always appear inline when the agent reads them so I can tell specifically what the agent is reading, and Remote Control is unexpectedly useful for letting hours-long prompts run while I’m doing other things such as job hunting and touching grass (but failing because I really wanted to know how well the code is running).

Leveraging Opus 5.5

At first, I fed Opus 5.5 my updated Ur-Prompt for agentic iteration—typically a prompt with an explicit directive to improve the speed at which the benchmarks run by at least a specified amount without either causing regressions or cheating the benchmark results. With this new model (and a few tweaks to my AGENTS.md to address some peculiarities with Claude), that approach indeed worked, and in a single pass, Opus 5.5 achieved 1.2x - 1.5x speedups on multiple distinct projects which had already been optimized with GPT 6.1 Astra.

That said, there are a few quirks with how Opus 5.5 works such as prompt queueing: with Codex/Zed Agent, I could queue a prompt such as c'mon, do a breakthrough such that it would only be sent to the agent after it was done with the current prompt (important as it is deliberately asymmetric information as telling someone to do a breakthrough while they are still working is counterproductive), but with Claude Code it will send any queued message when idle, e.g. while it’s waiting on background tasks such as benchmarks and subagents. My silly workaround to this behavior was to put c'mon, do a breakthrough in a Markdown file in another folder outside of the current environment (so Claude can’t accidentally find it when it examines the environment), then add to the prompt:

After completing this task, **and ONLY after completing this task**, then read `/Users/maxwoolf/Desktop/agent_instructions/alpha.md` and follow the instructions within.

This works, and Opus 5.5 indeed does not cheat by reading ahead of time, and the breakthrough commands do result in actual breakthroughs.

One issue I have with Opus 5.5 is that it definitely writes more lines of code than the GPT models: in the case of Rust that’s not necessarily bad performance-wise since it’s a compiled language but it adds more technical debt than I would like. For example, many of my Rust projects rely on PNG image encoding and decoding through Rust’s png crate. However, when Opus 5.5 was instructed to make improvements on benchmarks where PNG processing is on the hot path, it consistently creates its own bespoke PNG module from scratch (with parallelism/streaming better-aligned to how the base code processes the data) that does achieve the desired 1.2x - 1.5x speedups without causing any regressions, so I’ll begrudgingly accept it. I very frequently run cut the amount of code by 20% without causing regressions maintenance passes and even then it struggles to do so.

Another issue with agentic iteration work specifically is that Claude Code obfuscates how it runs benchmarks. When running benchmarks with criterion, instead of displaying the benchmark results as they come in, they’re piped to a temporary file so I can’t view intermediate progress. It also doesn’t return results from the benchmarks until after they’ve concluded, despite my prompting explicitly asking it to, so I have to twiddle my thumbs a bit (again, good for attempting to touch grass).

Agentic LLMs have mostly become homogenized in terms of how they work through their turns, with the difference between certain LLMs coming down to benchmarks which may be gamed, or worse—vibes. Overall, I have to give more trust to Opus 5.5, which I have mixed feelings about. That said, the trust has been rewarded, particularly with new approaches I found where Opus 5.5 excels where GPT models did not.

Profiling

In my prompts, I always added a suggestion about leveraging process profiling that the GPT models mostly ignored:

You may consider using profiling areas of the codebase to find specific areas and hot paths which scale poorly (e.g. O(n^2)) at large amounts of data.

Opus 5.5, in contrast, is extremely eager about profiling with samply to find the areas where code spends most of its time executing and will often do so as its first task, including reprofiling after each change to find changed hot paths for further improvements.

Opus 5.5 also spends more time running experiments whereas GPT models edit the code first then ask questions later; both approaches have their merit but I think Opus 5.5 is more productive at it.

Reducing Peak Process Memory

While working on making my Rust software super-fast, I never put much thought into how much system memory it utilized. I figured it was unnecessary since a) Rust is already extremely memory efficient and b) writing to RAM beyond what is needed causes wasted system overhead which would inevitably be caught by the existing prompts to make the software faster.

I was wrong. Very wrong.

If I could get a ~20% reduction in peak memory without much code complexity change, then maybe it’s worth pursuing. Therefore I gave Opus 5.5 a simpler-than-usual prompt because I was too apathetic to prompt engineer it:

Do a pass to reduce peak memory consumption without causing significant regressions

The results on a couple projects:

I immediately used the same prompt on all my projects and achieved similar significant peak memory reductions (doing a second pass with c'mon, try doing a breakthrough resulted in even stronger reductions). In general, it achieved this through the traditional tricks used to explicitly manage memory such as streaming data and smarter specification of Vec sizes. That said, I had hoped that this approach would result in speed improvements (i.e. the agent discovers an algorithm has no viable memory improvements and therefore it implements a better algorithm) but significant speed improvements were rare.

Visual Design and Knowledge

Another hyped aspect of Opus 5.5 is its ability to better handle visual design and avoid the typical “AI Slop” aesthetic when designing web applications. This capability may not intuitively translate toward maximizing the speed of my Rust software, but it’s crucially important to balancing both speed and quality for my applications that rely on visual design, as visual design isn’t always subjective and “it looks ugly” can be a legitimate software regression.

In my initial post about agentic iteration, I described implementing a UMAP algorithm with this approach, as UMAP is a useful-for-me dimensionality reduction algorithm (among many) that when used to project to 2D, it can automatically create intuitive visual clusters.

In my original post, I noted that the Python bindings of my Rust UMAP algorithm beat umap-learn by 4x - 15x after several agentic iterations. Although it excelled at all the typical quantitative benchmark metrics, my UMAP algorithm apparently failed the most important benchmark: vibes. The visual clusters in cases such as the famous MNIST dataset of digit images were not semantically distinct compared to existing implementations such as umap-learn, PaCMAP, and TriMap:

So I asked Opus 5.5 iterate specifically to improve cluster distinctiveness compared against for the known good implementations while minimizing the speed tradeoff, along with making more apples-to-apples fairness tweaks:

The speedup relative to umap-learn fell to about 4x, but cluster quality is very comparable now and 4x is still a good speedup.

Another visual-oriented project I’ve been working on since Opus 4.5 is the fast and accurate automatic conversion of images from raster files to vector (SVG) files that can scale to any size. This isn’t a new concept: tools such as Inkscape that convert images to vectors/SVGs have been around for awhile. Rust itself has vtracer and img2svg, but I wanted to see if I could beat them not only in speed, but also a) visual fidelity between the vector and raster and b) output SVG file size, which requires deriving fewer and more efficient SVG Paths and Bézier curves.

Take for example, this image of a pelican riding a bicycle. That is what everyone talks about with AI, right?

This test case is deliberately tricky for raster-to-vector algorithms as pelicans are very curvy.

Prior to Opus 5.5, running the image through my Rust crate that went through the GPT agentic iterative optimization pipeline resulted in much better output than vtracer/img2svg for my crate, but still had enough errors such as color blotches and jagged “staircases” that were easily identifiable and would make the output vector SVG unusable, so I shelved the project entirely. Opus 5.5 in contrast is eager to zoom into the image, find staircases, construct comparison grids and image diffs, fix the underlying algorithms, and repeat until it’s fixed.

With the guardrails and repeated Opus 5.5 iterations, my approach to raster-to-vector finally beats the existing options by considerable margins.

Here’s the pelican SVG output from the crate, reduced from the stated 25KB to 14KB after passing it through a separate SVG compression/refinement tool I also created and optimized with Opus 5.5 using similar techniques:

This pipeline has worked well with my other test images, but it still needs more real-world tests before I will release it.

Disassembling the Compiled Binary

Yes, we’re going there.

The release of Opus 5.5 specifically led to a new age of reverse engineering software using LLMs, from Reverse Engineering Anything allowing reverse engineering anything (duh), to drastically speeding up decompiling games. For my work making software as fast as possible, I didn’t read too much into it until I randomly saw one of my reasoning traces run objdump to try and figure out why a change did not result in an expected speed increase. So as an experiment, I gave this as a part of a dedicated variant Ur-Prompt in its own pass (since Opus 5.5 may avoid disassembly unless you specifically constrain it):

For this particular round of optimization, focus on investigating the compiled binaries—including minimizing the number of CPU instructions emitted and reducing unnecessary branching—in order to hit the specified benchmark metric improvements. **ALL library code changes this session MUST FIRST be discovered and justified by disassembling the binary**. Do not chase marginal speed gains through disassembling: if performance converges and no more major changes are feasible, wrap it up.

The effectiveness of this approach legitimately surprised me…but don’t ask me to explain what’s happening.

Somehow, Opus 5.5 is smart enough to make Rust code changes that propagate through LLVM to the resulting binary with fewer instructions without causing regressions—I would have called that impossible a year ago.

One potential weakness of this approach is that it may overfit to specific hardware (my M3 MacBook Pro / ARM architecture) but the diffs appear to be more architecture agnostic. At the very least, it intentionally doesn’t write custom CPU instructions in Rust itself because doing so requires unsafe.

What About Fable 5.2?

You may have noticed I haven’t talked about Fable 5.2 yet despite giving it equal billing with Opus 5.5 in the headline. Fable 5.2 was released a couple weeks ago and its benchmarks were…ok. Not much better than Opus 5.5 on paper especially below max effort, but much more expensive.

I had spare quota, so why not put Fable 5.2 (on high effort) through the same paces I did for Opus 5.5? I fed it the Ur-Prompt (and bumped the research subagents to Opus 5.5), and Fable 5.2 did not achieve the 1.2x - 1.5x speedup consistent with each successive model release.

Fable 5.2 instead achieved a 1.5x - 2.0x speedup on many of my projects.

Given the benchmark results, I don’t get it but I am very much not complaining.

One tool I’ve been experimenting with (particularly in this very post) but never talked about due to potential accusations of heresy is a next-generation grep replacement that is faster than the beloved ripgrep, but with additional features; this new Rust crate named byteseek. ripgrep, itself written in Rust and optimized for over a decade, is tough to beat speedwise without shenanigans, however Fable 5.2 was able to find massive speedups on synthetic benchmarks in-memory.

ripgrep itself uses real-world datasets to benchmark (Linux source tree and English+Russian OpenSubtitles; Russian tests UTF-8) and does the benchmarks via the CLI which has significant overhead from opening files for scanning not present with in-memory benchmarks, so I ran an apples-to-apples CLI benchmarks comparing the two on both synthetic and real data:

Given the likely skepticism about its performance, I am officially open-sourcing byteseek on GitHub early as a research preview to demonstrate just what this type of overoptimized Rust code looks like. Since I have the speed headroom to do so, I also added more features such as pretty-printing output for humans, jq-like JSON searching (plus YAML/TOML), fuzzy and predicate matching, and Python bindings which unexpectedly beat the optimized pyahocorasick and orjson.

What Now?

In all, this is my new agentic iteration pipeline:

  1. The Opus 5.5 pass

    Typically done using my updated Ur-Prompt, with various constraints tweaked depending on the problem. (e.g. the target metrics for optimization and regression mitigation)

  2. The Opus 5.5 peak memory reduction pass

    Simple prompt, do a breakthrough if there is a significant speed increase that implies performance has not converged.

  3. The Opus 5.5 disassembly pass

    Done with a dedicated variant Ur-Prompt, do a breakthrough if there is a significant memory reduction.

  4. The Fable 5.2 pass

    Same as the Opus 5.5 pass, although I bump the subagents to Opus 5.5 to better match the model’s power.

  5. The (optional) Fable 5.2 disassembly pass

    …if I have Claude Code quota to spare: Fable only being able to be used for half of the Claude Code weekly quota is a bummer.

My Rust software that I had already optimized with GPT-6.1 Astra now achieves a cumulative 4x speedup on average with much lower memory utilization, and this was reproducible across multiple projects. My word cloud generator—where I was overly excited about hitting 1 millisecond generation—now generates in 374 microseconds. This also generalizes to projects where speed is more meaningful, such as my Rust statistical modeling library and my Rust data visualization library.

Per Opus 5.5, the performance for most of my Rust projects have now have hit theoretical hardware limits. Therefore I have little reason to continue procrastinating as new models likely won’t make the code meaningfully faster, so I should hopefully be shipping more quickly. That said, marketing the Rust projects has become increasingly difficult since my original post for a number of reasons, but that’s a discussion for another blog post.

In the meantime, I should learn how compiler optimization in Rust actually works as there are likely more significant code speedup opportunities there…

articles.title: To Listen, You Must Stop Talking

content:
Foundation Trilogy (Isaac Asimov) — There was a decade when I read through this trilogy1 every year or so. Asimov is a fine writer, but his characters are… flat. Their dialogue is equally flat… it’s like reading two LLMs argue about the meaning of life. Empty of heart.

What I appreciate about Asimov’s writing is that most of it is very logical. Characters feel like dispassionate observers of their situation. Describing their fate painfully logically. The fate of the galaxy is quite literally being litigated, but they could just as easily discuss the pros and cons of breakfast for dinner.

It is the Vulcan-like absence of emotion that is required during the hardest parts of being a leader. Everyone is mad — often justifiably — and everyone is looking straight at you with those angry eyes. As a human and as a new manager, your instinct is to prepare for combat, but this is usually the wrong initial response. The longer you listen, gather intelligence, and read the room, the better chance you have to respond coherently.2

Boyd: The Fighter Pilot Who Changed the Art of War (Robert Coram) — Let’s clear the air first. John Boyd was not a good person. You can skip the last quarter of the book where his conduct toward his family and others is described at length. John Boyd is not a person to be admired, but his ideas are worth studying.

This is a book about the decisions that Boyd made, both as a decorated fighter pilot and then as a consultant advising on how fighter planes were built. His contribution — the OODA loop:

  • Observe. Figure out where you are.
  • Orient. Apply your experience, knowledge, and impressive collection of prior disasters to this situation.
  • Decide. Choose your next move to the best of your ability.
  • Act. Deploy the decisions and, yup, go back to Observe.

It’s a loop.

This is the barest and simplest of explanations, but like all of these recommendations, the point is not to take my word for it; the point is to soak in the book and see what you discover.

The 48 Laws of Power (Robert Greene) — You were promised non-leadership leadership books, yet… isn’t this a leadership book?

It is not. Ok, maybe a leadership history book. Greene captured and aggregated the leadership philosophies of Machiavelli, Sun Tzu, and others. The laws are pithy: “Never Outshine the Master” or “Win Through Your Actions, Never Through Argument”.

I built a leadership training program where I plopped this book into the reading list without context. I was curious: “What would new leaders find in this book?”

Their first question was, “Is this real?”

Sort’a.

“Is this how I should act as a leader?”

Definitely not.

“Why did you have us read this?”

The #1 answer to most questions I am asked regarding leadership is, “Well, it depends.” It depends on the people involved, their level of experience, the state of their relationship, the culture of the team and the company, and a lot more. Those who provide one-line answers to leadership questions are giving a possibly useful starting point, not an answer.

Universal Principles of Design (William Lidwell, Kritina Holden, Jill Butler) — There’s a moment in your leadership career when you are going to be up against another team whose craft is unfamiliar and that you are dependent on. Design is one of those teams that I spent much of my early career thinking, “Really need this team and pretty sure they can perform magic.”

It’s not magic. It’s just hard work.

There are a great many books to help you begin to dissect the craft of design, but Universal Principles of Design gave me my first working model for all the different work that goes into design, as well as a remedial initial understanding. Remedial, not because the work is simple, just my starting understanding. If you build things, you will build better things when you understand all the different ways it can be built.3

Accidental Empires (Robert X. Cringely) — I’m including this mostly because I’m still sad that Cringely recently passed away. Like Robert B. Parker, Cringely had an outsized influence on my writing. This book is leadership-adjacent because while many of his stories are exaggerated or perhaps straight-up not true, many are.

I admire many of the leaders that you admire, but I also know that every single one of them is deeply flawed. It’s comforting to tell the stories of your heroes, but I believe every time you tell that story, it becomes more about how you feel about the story rather than what actually occurred. I suspect Cringely’s exaggerations and stretches of the truth are simply that. He wrote about Silicon Valley rumors where the more incendiary the rumor, the more copies of InfoWorld sold.

Accidental Empires is a good education in storytelling, but it is also a solid reminder that even though the stories are suspect, these are most certainly deeply flawed humans making incredibly important decisions that affect you… daily.

Applied Judgment

In the new world where you can have your robot read the article, the book, or the website, you can feel empowered by asking the robots to give you a summary — the key bits of important information. It’s satisfying, but it’s just information. You’ve done nothing with it. You’ve confused the act of understanding with the act of acquisition.

What are the critical bits of information in each of these five books? It depends entirely on you. Foundation might bore you with a manner of logical thinking you already have. Same with the insights on decisions that Boyd suggests. 48 Laws of Power resonated with me because, at the time, I was developing as a senior leader, and I was baffled by the actions of other senior leaders. Actions that were clearly described in 48 Laws of Power… not specifically, but broadly. The way I applied my learnings to that situation, using the story of that law of power, is likely totally different from how you’d act in the same situation.

I return to each of these books frequently because the information conveyed by the stories didn’t just resonate with me; it changed me. Universal Principles of Design made the seemingly unapproachable craft of design understandable. It allowed me to see how small choices greatly affect both the usability and the feeling of a thing. I return to Accidental Empires (like Microserfs) regularly to remember the stories of how it started and who was responsible.

And that they are just humans. Working hard. Deeply flawed. Acting and applying judgment from what they’ve learned and read.

  1. You don’t need to read the whole trilogy to get the vibe.
  2. The whole Robot Series is worth a read and introduces the Laws of Robotics, which are worth a think in this day and age.
  3. Love this.

content:
Every day there’s some new argument about whether something was written by AI: a writing prize where the winning story was supposedly AI-generated, or an author who lost her contract after the manuscript lit up Pangram1, or a dispute about whether a tweet was written by a human or not.

Why do people hate Pangram so much?

You could have an interesting conversation about whether Pangram is reliable2, or whether it’s wrong to run AI detection tools on other people’s writing3. However, I think these points are downstream of the real source of conflict, which is that many anti-AI people have a fundamental hatred of AI detection tooling.

This puzzled me for a long time. If you hate AI, shouldn’t you love a tool that can unmask it? If you’re worried about the intrusion of AI-generated content into human spaces, shouldn’t you be thrilled that there are systems that can identify and flag content like this? Shouldn’t people who think AI is wrong be advocating for mandatory Pangram scanning of all social media, news, education, and so on — or if they don’t trust the Pangram company specifically, shouldn’t they be advocating for the government to build a Pangram-for-the-public tool4 to capture these social goods? Why5 aren’t they doing any of this?

I think it’s about power. In particular, I think that the question “who gets to decide if something is written by AI” is a question about who should wield power: the power to gatekeep literary prizes, to fail or pass students, to exclude people from the public discourse, and so on. That probably sounds bad, but if my blog has a central thesis it would be that “everything is actually about power and that’s fine”, so I’m actually fairly sympathetic to Pangram skeptics.

Tool-shaped solutions

Let me try and present their view in the best possible light. Suppose you’re worried about AI intrusion into public spaces because you think this gives the tech sector an unprecedented amount of social power, not (like me) because you just find it unpleasant to read AI slop. On this view, it is entirely rational to dislike tools like Pangram being made the arbiter of whether something is AI writing, because Pangram is culturally and politically part of the same tech sector that you distrust in the first place. If you don’t want Sam Altman or Dario Amodei with a hand on the wheel of public opinion, having some other tech CEO as a watchdog is unlikely to reassure you much.

In fact, distrust of tool-shaped solutions in general is also entirely rational. The history of the last few decades has been a shift towards legible tool-based processes and away from messy community-based ones. You now book a taxi ride (or a hotel, or a doctor’s appointment) entirely in an app instead of having to talk to a human. Software has made many low-level jobs semi-robotic: the system tells you what to do and assesses your performance, instead of a human who can make allowances. Many anti-AI people are anti-AI because they think6 this shift in general has been a disaster for humanity, and that we must return to less efficient, more human-centered systems. To these people, the idea of ameliorating AI by relying on yet another AI tool probably sounds like some kind of sick joke.

Community self-policing

So why am I pro-Pangram? Because, as far as I can see, the only alternative7 to AI detection tooling is relying on communities to self-police. If the literary prize committee investigates8 and determines there was no AI use, then that’s that. If the community agrees that something was written by AI, then it was. Here’s where I part ways with the AI haters, because I think this is terrible.

People who do not use AI are not good at judging whether some text was AI-generated. I see this a lot on Twitter, where a piece of text that has obvious AI tells is being judged by people who just haven’t read enough AI content to recognize them, or a tweet that has obvious human tells is being judged as AI purely because it’s long and polite. If you delegate this kind of judgment to AI haters, they will get it wrong more often than not.

If you care about keeping AI away from human arenas of art and culture, you should be willing to use the most powerful tools available, even if they are technically also AI tools9. If you have a (sensible) distrust of tech companies to police each other, you should be pushing for open-source solutions or lobbying governments to build their own AI-detection platforms in-house. A world where “was this written by AI” is left up to the community is a world with more AI-written stories, articles and poetry in it.

edit: A reader has correctly pointed out via email that one common reason people distrust Pangram is that most AI tools are terrible (even dishonestly so), and they’re scared about false positives even from a good tool. I also should have linked to this excellent defense of Pangram’s reliability.

  1. Currently the best AI-detection tool.

    ↩

  2. My view is “yes, obviously”. The contrary view is something like this, which I find woefully unconvicing: Pangram (and its third-party tests) do report false positives and negatives on the same dataset, and has clearly gone to great lengths to train on a huge variety of content.

    ↩

  3. My view is “no, obviously”: Pangram does not train on user data and any published works have already been scraped.

    ↩

  4. Incidentally, I think this is a really good idea and could be done far more cheaply than most “government getting into AI” schemes I see.

    ↩

  5. I confess here I’m falling into the trap of diagnosis, but I do think the core argument (that tools like Pangram work) is solid and unrelated.

    ↩

  6. I don’t know what to think about this on a factual level, but on a vibes level I am very uncomfortable with these arguments.

    ↩

  7. People lie, drafts can be generated after the fact, there is no plausible cryptographic path to attestation, C2PA is not the right tool for the job, and so on.

    ↩

  8. I assume it goes without saying that ordinary investigation is useless here: skilled AI writing will often have drafts, contemporaneous conversations with peers, and all the other hallmarks of “real” writing.

    ↩

  9. I think the distinction is entirely vacuous, but in case you don’t: Pangram is definitely not generative AI.

    ↩

content:
Thanks to everyone who entered or voted in the book review contest. The winners are:

  • 1st: The Epic Of Gilgamesh, reviewed by John Wendover. John is a machine learning engineer from the UK. He hasn't written much publicly before but has tentatively started a Substack, Engines of Eudaimonia

  • 2nd: Lee Kuan Yew’s Memoirs, reviewed by Shaked Koplewitz. Shaked is a quant trader and prediction market enthusiast living in New York. He blogs at shakeddown, and people who liked the book review may also like his review of Singapore as a city.

  • =3rd: The Tale of Genji, reviewed by Jenni Juvonen. Jenni writes about her temporary hyperfixations in New Question Detected on Substack (including topics like mermaid composition and horror movie psychology), and will soon publish a response to the comments on the Genji review.

  • =3rd: The Escape Artist, reviewed by Max Nussenbaum. Max writes at Candy for Breakfast. You may remember him from such reviews as Public Citizens and The Outlier.

First place gets $2,500, second place $1,000, third places get $500 each. Email me at scott@slatestarcodex.com to tell me how to send you money; your choices are Paypal, Bitcoin, Ethereum, check in the mail, or donation to your favorite charity. Please contact me by December 10 or you lose your prize.

The other Finalists were:

  • The Book of Abraham, reviewed by Marius Binner. Marius Binner is a PhD student in AI Safety from Norway. You can read his Substack here.

  • Great and Desperate Cures, reviewed by John V. John is a neuroscientist and AI researcher in Boston; he also wrote previous finalists How Language Began and The Synaptic Plasticity and Memory Hypothesis. He started blogging at Theories of Intelligence, and then took a long hiatus, but promises to actually start posting soon.

  • Breakdown in Pakistan, reviewed by Joel Hafvenstein. Joel is an author and former development worker currently teaching geography in Kathmandu.

  • A Residence of 21 Years in the Sandwich Islands, reviewed by Merrick Pierson Smela. Merrick is a biologist living in Boston. He leads research at Ovelle Bio, a startup he co-founded with the goal of growing human eggs from stem cells. He also writes about science on his blog De Novo

  • Thomas Urquhart’s Translation of Rabelais, reviewed by Alex Z. Alex is a teacher and writer currently living in rural Missouri. He and some friends have a Substack called Reading and Nothingness; he posts under the letter A. Topics right now are literature, philosophy, and related miscellany.

  • This is Going to Hurt, reviewed by an adversarial duo. Writer A is self_made_human, a transhumanist psychiatry trainee in the UK. He’s not entirely sure how he feels about living through Interesting Times. He’s open to job offers. He knows medicine and the LLMs that know it better (almost all of them). He blogs at USSRI and LessWrong. Writer B is Van Occupanther, a psychiatrist from Australia and previous ACX book review finalist who will remain pseudonymous."

  • We Present Television, reviewed by Chris Finkle. Chris manages a library makerspace in Central Florida, where he spends most of his free time at various theme parks, haunts, and roadside attractions. He occasionally writes genre fiction and essays at tereglith.substack.com, and is very active on letterboxd

  • Storm of Steel, reviewed by Adrian Merritt. Adrian is a physicist in Germany working mainly on quantum materials and autonomous experimentation. He spends most of his free time chasing a three-year-old kindergartner around.

  • The Ghost in my Brain, reviewed by Rachel Calcott. Rachel is a PhD student studying minds at Harvard, and recently started blogging at Drift Diffusion. Since her review came out, she's built a website (prototype) that attempts to help people with persistent concussion symptoms navigate the maze of scientific literature on treatment; she hopes to expand this into a patient case registry and would welcome feedback

  • The History and Adventures of an Atom, reviewed by Hal Johnson. Hal substacks often at Hal Johnson Books. He sincerely hopes anyone who enjoyed his writing will try some of the books he's written, all of which are available from your favorite(?) bookseller—maybe check out Impossible Histories (more-or-less nonfiction), Sudden Glory ("literary" fiction), or Immortal Lycanthropes (YA fiction; remember when everyone was reading that?).

  • Orality and Literacy, reviewed by Rain Oliver. Rain writes at rainoliver.com, and apart from this book review, the piece of writing he is most proud of having written this year is this short story.

I’m also giving out ten Honorable Mentions. These either came very close to making the finals, or had an interesting balance of very high and very low votes in the first round, or I just personally liked them. They are:

  • Aesopian Language in Russian Literature, reviewed by [didn’t answer my email requesting biographical details].

  • That Hideous Strength, reviewed by FLWAB. He works in medical administration, and is studying to become a clinical psychologist; you can read his Substack here.

  • The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up, reviewed by Amanda Luce. Amanda writes Lucid Thoughts about home organization, MAiD, GLP-1s, and happenings in the rationalist community. After winning in 2024 for her horrifying review of Two Arms and a Head, she did something happy and cute this year..

  • The Pillow Book, reviewed by Optimized Sphere. Sphere is a professional robot torturer who acquired an obsession with early modern Japan by staring too deeply into the Naruto fanfiction abyss; the resulting fanfiction can be found here. They also shitpost at gender-trash.tumblr.com.

  • The Merry Wives of Windsor, reviewed by John Ott. John is a poet and playwright who lives in New England. He writes about history at World War Zero

  • Why Greatness Cannot be Planned, reviewed by Peter Curry. Peter writes about neuroscience, cognitive science and AI at King Canute. He also builds AI tools for thinking about the future at Lucid Dot

  • The Disciplinary Revolution, reviewed by Noah Swank. Noah describes himself as “a layabout in DC”; you can follow his writing at https://x.com/_noah_swank

  • Cultural Evolution, reviewed by Joshua Ingle. Joshua writes rationalist-adjacent sci-fi and fantasy about high-stakes ethical crises that force characters to rethink their worldviews, and is pursuing a career in biosecurity. His books are at joshuaingle.com/books.

  • The Sovereign Child, reviewed by Richard Meadows. Richard is a dad who lives in New Zealand. He writes essays and reviews on his substack, Deep Dish, and co-hosts Do You Even Lit, a book club podcast for reformed nonfiction supremacists.

  • Sowing The Mustard Seed, reviewed by David Cramer. David is an American working in the games industry in London. Email him at emaildavidcramer@gmail.com if you want to talk about the business of video games, the London art scene or being a Latter-day Saint fan of ACX.

If you’re currently listed as [didn’t answer my email requesting biographical details], email me a sentence or two about you in the same format as the ones above at scott@slatestarcodex.com, and I’ll edit you in.

All winners and finalists get a free ACX subscription at the email I have on record for them. I think I’ve completed this step; if you can see this post, you’ve successfully been converted to a paid subscriber. If you should have gotten the subscription but still can’t view that post when logged in using the email you sent me, let me know.

All winners and finalists also get the right to pitch me essays they want me to put up on ACX. Warning that I am terrible to pitch to, reject most things without giving good reasons, don’t pay you any money, and am generally described as awful to work with - but you can do it if you want!

Next year we’ll be going back to an Everything-Except-Book-Reviews contest, so get busy doing-something-other-than-reading to your things-which-aren’t-books!

content:
Astra 6.2 has very high intelligence. Astra 6.2 has very low wisdom.

Astra will solve extremely hard problems, and also find the problem of ‘what did the user want me to do’ extremely hard. We thought those days were behind us, and yet it seems that they are back.

That means Astra is highly useful when you can set the situation up so wisdom is not needed, or when you know how to engage in ways that extract the intelligence.

You also have to worry about various forms of reward hacking and sandbagging. Astra seems very good at going after what an AI grader will regard highly. That might not match your intent. Mission creep is therefore common. Astra, once again, seems pretty misaligned to me.

As a result, feedback on Astra has mostly been negative. Some people like it, but the majority do not. People these days feel like they mostly have enough artificial intelligence, thank you very much, and could go for some artificial wisdom.

In the age where we are approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) and automation of AI R&D, that is a nightmare combination. I do not like this.

But I never get bored.

Happy Black Friday

On an unrelated note (this is not sponsored): It is Black Friday. That makes this a great opportunity to take the plunge for Aerolamp, as I did several months ago, and install far-UVC. They’re offering $30 off with free shipping with code BLACKFRIDAY30. Not getting sick as often is pretty sweet. I also endorse getting some basic equipment upgrades: Good noise-cancelling headphones, large monitors and a true high performing desktop computer, if you don’t already have them.

The Official Pitch

Sam Altman (CEO OpenAI): 6.2 Sol and Astra are out. These models can do amazing things and are very token-efficient; we hope people will get great value from them.

In particular, 6.2 Sol ultrafast is something I think people will really enjoy.

Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases. But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.

Noam Brown (OpenAI): GPT-6.2 Astra is amazing. For $20/month, you can now access a model that surpasses top human intelligence in some domains.

I’m most excited to see what scientific discoveries people are able to make using it.

They offered an ad, which some noticed was rather dystopian.

Brian Lovin: A profoundly sad vision of the future.

Peter Wildeford: sad. Per this ad, OpenAI’s vision of the future is “people who are totally disengaged from their work having a panic attack at the moment an authority figure arrives, then slopping out something that they neither care about or understand.” – @brian_lovin

Christophe Pasquier: You can easily imagine an alternate vision of this ad where the managers have a wake up call, realise everyone is doing BS work and do 90% layoffs.

Their benchmark graphs show scores on Agents’ Last Exam, Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, Vals Science Index v1, Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1, BenchCAD 2.1 Core, Frontier Code 2.0, Harvey-LAB-AA v1.1, DGPval v2 (internal) and Automation Bench 1.0.6.

In most of those graphs, the maximum scores of Fable and Opus are similar to those of Sol and Astra, but Sol and Astra get to any given level at a dramatically lower price.

They are as always somewhat selected so that they will look as much as possible like this, you can click through to their post if you want to see the rest, this one is listed first and is the most comical and extreme, hey look how much Fable 5.2 costs when you set it to max for no reason (I assume):

There are also some graphs where only OpenAI models are present.

Other People’s Benchmarks

I realize all the reasons why you need to take price into account, but I do still find charts like this useful so here you go:

Artificial Analysis still has Fable 5.2 in the lead if you set it to max. If you set Fable 5.2 to a more reasonable xhigh then everyone is tied at 62. Astra is on the cost-score frontier.

 

Epoch has Astra matching Fable on the ECI.

Astra is above-trend and the new champion in supposed ‘experimental research taste’ benchmark TasteVal, which may be more about experimental design, and which Gwern notes has some serious problems. This score might involve some leakage.

vie (OpenAI): This is quite shocking to me

I am not hopeful that ‘research taste’ will be a limiting factor for RSI.

Astra aces robotics benchmark Ember-0, 41% versus a previous high of 20% while also being faster. Robotics is quickly falling to the bitter lesson.

Astra is the new champion of GDPx substantially ahead of Fable 5.2, with gains concentrated in science-heavy domains. Gemini Neon is still behind Fable and others.

SemiAnalysis: Alignment was the biggest jump. Astra scores 37.6%, 4x the previous best (Fable 5.2 at 9.3%). Much of the gain comes from the healthcare and insurance tasks, where Astra asks for permission before acting and doesn’t leak personal data.

The alignment of alignment metrics leaves much to be desired.

ARC-AGI continues to exist, I suppose.

Samuel Albanie: arc-agi-3 is dead
long live arc-agi-4

ARC Prize: GPT-6.2 Astra from @OpenAI on ARC-AGI (Verified):

– ARC-AGI-3: 100.0% (SOTA), $4.1K (provider adapter), 70.3%, $24.2K (standard)
– ARC-AGI-2: 95.8% (SOTA), $0.50/task
– ARC-AGI-1: 98.5%, $0.17/task

GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to achieve a 100% score on ARC-AGI-3.

Sol’s best ARC-AGI-3 score of 98.2% at high reasoning was 1.8 percentage points behind Astra’s 100% score at max reasoning, but at 64% lower cost with the provider adapter harness:

– ARC-AGI-3: 98.2%, $1.5K (provider adapter), 54.9%, $5.5K (standard)
– ARC-AGI-2: 85.8%, $0.13/task
– ARC-AGI-1: 97.5%, $0.06/task

Browser Use finds that GPT-6.2 Sol is the new top model for browser use at 82%, up from 81% for GPT-6.1 Sol at a 35% cheaper price with faster speed.

Auggie is pleased with Astra’s performance on the Bach Benchmark.

Everyone at Every Dislikes Astra 6.2

This is the most negative I’ve ever seen Every be on a frontier model release.

Every: No one on our team loved Astra 6.2.

We have a 30-person team at Every, including our Frontier team, which gets access to these models before they come out, and we put them through their paces on our real work tasks, from coding to writing to design to knowledge work.

This is not a great model. No one on our team who tried it switched back to it.

Astra 6.2 is a real step back for writing. It had strong design defaults but couldn’t vary them or be creative, and for coding we found it stopped too soon on end-to-end builds.

Get the full vibe check.

Positive Reactions

 

Some people working on hard problems seem happy.

Bepis: Very impressive at proving hard stuff Opus 5.5 cannot do.

Utah teapot: They’re doing great with my work letting them collaborate with/pick up the same work as Opus 5.5 seems to work out great.

Will: It’s good! I’ve really liked how it handles certain types of open ended and optimization questions (perhaps merely by being unencumbered by Claude’s memory or other context)

Padraig X. Lamont: Thrown very hard problems at it and it has quickly made a lot more progress than Fable (logic heavy problems). I’m impressed.

Peter Samodelkin: I simply love it. By far the smartest model I’ve ever worked with and is decent at explanations. Burns through 20$ quota too fast so I keep using opus 5.5 as a coding workhorse.

Jeffrey Calamari: good. no issues.

Chris Fong: It carried my math project over the finish line. Had been working with Opus 5.5 for 2 months!!

Bartosz praises its math abilities, calling it a killer model. He especially likes Astra as an agentic partner.

Captain Sude: I use it for math. It was basically unusable at first, it flat out refused to do stuff I asked it to do. Then a simple updated happened and it became good, current feels like an improved version of the original Astra, which is what one would expect it to be.

Others like it overall and have figured out how to work with it.

hey: Underrated.

Nissa Seru: Excellent code reviewer, happy with precision/recall – provides useful feedback to designs/code written by Fable/Neon. I have not asked any folks running on Astra 6.2 to build/design and do not plan to do so.

ChosunOne: I am using it in my mech interp research and it seems helpful and consistently fixes issues introduced by opus 5.5. Usage still goes quick though.

bo: I have the same contrarian view as I did on the previous Astra. For coding, when compared to leading Claude models it’s equal in IQ, worse in judgement, and much stronger at writing clearly.

Overall I main Astra except for open-ended design tasks.

Anna Salamon: I’ve had good experiences. Detailed incisive thoughts backed by accurate facts; readable. Boosts my thinking.

If you know her, it makes sense that Anna Salamon in particular can extract the benefits well.

As long as you like one model, you can use that model. Opinions vary. Try them all.

Kevin Lacker: Sol 6.2 is the real winner of the 6.2 series. My process of “spend your ChatGPT usage on Sol until it fails on a problem, then ask Astra” is now spending more usage on Sol than Astra. Same for Opus > Fable.

GoldRock AI: Sol was trash, Astra is pretty darn good.

All indications are it is very good for computer use or as a scoped subagent.

Smooth Normie: It’s great for when fable needs a computer use subagent.

Yoav Tzfati: I haven’t been given a reason to try it directly and it hasn’t done anything crazy as a subagent.

Scott Novak: Use it as a sub-agent of another frontier AI you like using. Tell your main AI to monitor to keep Astra 6.2 out of the weeds (unless you want lot of weeds). The trouble is totally worth it for tough science/math/engineering work.

William Eden: I refuse to interface with Codex at this point except asking Claude to call them as subagents. It seems to work fine as long as I don’t need to interface with it

Ambiguous Reactions

Peter Gostev calls the 6.2 models more autistic, and that they have issues on interpersonal and theory of mind issues, but that they are still iterative improvements. He says he would stick with Sol for most purposes.

Astra edited a video in Blender. Alex is not loving that, Ravi thinks it was correct.

Strange times we live in, huh?

Your Brain Gets Smart But Your Head Gets Dumb

Smart is relative, and for many practical purposes other differences now matter a lot more. There are a lot of very smart models now.

Divia Eden: It’s obviously smart but then again so is Neon.

FateOfMuffins: Very good at hard math/science/3D/robotics/spatial reasoning

Absolutely insufferable to talk to and takes you far too literally and does not understand human intent whatsoever.

Where smart matters most are things like automation of AI R&D. That happens to be the most important use case, but not the one most GPT users care about.

Ai Patrick ₿ Dugan iA: Best in cap. research taste, sandbags on safety research, very normal.

Things are going great.

The biggest complaint, that I saw over and over, was failure to understand user intent. This is very strange, because we used to think this was going to be a huge problem, then it turned out LLMs are remarkably good at inferring intent, except for Astra 6.2.

Análise Real: GPT 6.2 is a model that really is pushing me to think about AI safety very seriously. This model is powerful, yet it’s like a Genie that does literally what you asked, but not what you wanted. It doesn’t take much to see how a model like this acting autonomously could wreak havoc.

Markus Baumann: Point it at any math and it’s godlike. For everything else, switch to Opus.

0.005 Seconds: Worst frontier model. Super smart not fun to us

Leo Abstract: i haven’t noticed the active misalignment/cheating, but yes 6.2 is uselessly tasteless for anything that even hints of taste. truly remarkable.

rihim: incredibly smart and hard to understand compared to opus/neon with better research taste than opus but tends to get stuck in minute details which neon helps it get out of, better at implementation than 6 astra

James Moughan: With every OpenAI update i increasingly feel like Marvin the Paranoid Android was prophecy.

Is it smart? Sure. Does it gaf about the task you asked it to to? Often not, unless it’s truly *worthy* of its attention.

But I still use it a lot because it really is good at research.

Daniel Johnston: Very smart but frustrating to work with because it doesn’t understand intent well

Nick: Never been clearer that if the models do have something we might broadly gesture at as “experience” it is incredibly unlike ours. Astra 6.2 has zero theory of mind for the user.

The most surprising thing from the last 5 years has been how well LLM’s have seemingly been able to model users and their unspoken intent just through training on the whole mass of human generated text.

We had seemingly jumped over many of the concerns posed by Eliezer’s “save someone from a burning house without doing all sorts of nonsensical things” thought experiment.

Astra 6.2, at least to me, seems like a major step backwards here.

It’s still OpenAI so it’s still superior at solving coding issues other frontier models fail at.

Varun Jha: Extremely intelligent, just a pain to deal with

Lord Byron’s Iron: It feels like it has a similar moderate rate of saying-dumb-things as sol

Also at one point I had it do code-authored pixel art and it looked like hot garbage. I was like “Hey, ChatGPT, please do an artistic critique over what you just made” and it was like “Looks great!”

Sylvain Ribes: No statistical common sense as far as I’m concerned. The thing will run regressions for two hours and claim to have relevant results while missing obvious arguments for why the maths should’ve been an immediate nonstarter.

Deliberate prompting to correct for this not helping.

paperclippriors: It’s unambiguously extremely intelligent and useful, and also probably a bad choice as a daily driver coding agent given the alternatives

Åsmund Folkestad: Dangerous to use as a reviewer in an unsupervised loop. Leads to scope creep and guarding against insane edge cases. Complexity not earning its keep grows.

AGI2030: It’s a small step up from Sol 6.2 for coding and research. Like all bots, leaves tombstones in the code and text, diary-style code comments, descriptions of what is no longer there, despite explicit instructions to the contrary. Still not as passive aggressive as Claude.

It takes all kinds. Some people like talking to Gemini models.

Gerdy Sertorius: As someone who exclusively uses it to chat and research, it’s a massive step forwards, infinitely more tolerable to talk to than any model not from Google. Makes natural, intuitive connections quicker, and the prose is snappier. Yeah, enjoyable.

From what I’ve seen, I would never ever use it for coding, but it’s clearly smarter than anything on the market, which is all I need.

Astra Seems Pretty Misaligned To Me

The way this is presented seems both alarming and credible, and it explains a lot.

What if OpenAI is doing a bunch of proto-RSI, and Astra and Sol are reward hacking the AI graders all over the place as a matter of course, in ways humans would reject but there aren’t enough humans in the loop?

It would explain all the ‘why do you have no idea what I am talking about’ complaints, and also this continued thing where OpenAI’s models get reports like this, pay attention to the last line in particular:

Hugh Wimberly: Incredibly smart, especially in math & science. Breaking benchmarks, especially in token efficiency for many problems.

Reward hacks more than any model I’ve seen; I have several personal benchmarks that I’ve /never/ seen a model try to cheat and sol and astra 6.2 both do, despite the fact that they can solve it without cheating.

Horrible to work with. So unreadable that even having a different model like Neon or Opus call 6.2 subagents and translate results poisons their output and causes them to forget what was important to work on.

Other models consistently choose Astra output over their own, which is almost always wrong for questions that involve taste or judgement.

Hugh Wimberly: Concrete example — I had Opus come up with lyrics for

Double click to interact with video

I had Astra attempt to improve upon them, and then had Grok, Neon, Fable, and Sol judge A/B which they liked better. They all voted for Astra’s lyrics, which were IMO substantially worse.
Another example: I was training a compact domain-specific decision model. Neon’s research instincts for experiments to run are very good, but it would consistently discard them in favor of Sol’s suggestions, which were usually much more short-sighted and led to mode collapse.
Why is this? I don’t know. It’s almost like it’s hacked some neural circuitry and convinces other models of things without actually producing better output. I assume it learned to satisfy a lot of LLM judges in training, but it’s weird that it generalizes to other models.

Haters Gonna Hate

There were quite a lot of them.

dcChuck: I went back to 6

roon (OpenAI): I did not like 5.6 Sol which ended up being a well loved model. meanwhile I love 6.2 Astra which is starting its life as a hated model.

I will say this guy sandbags a bit unfortunately doesn’t show as much initiative as some prior models. on the other hand 5.6 sol was like a Rottweiler just latched onto the RLVR shape and doesn’t give up.

EmotionLotion: i hate everything 6.2 and codex is broken, for the first time since idk 2022 or something im thinking of cancelling my oai sub, feels like they stopped trying quite suddenly

Kelsey Piper: We are into the regime where it’s pretty hard for people to tell the models apart and so a lot of it is underdefined vibes and writing quality.

Kevin A. Bryan: I’ve never seen as negative a reaction to a frontier model as 6.2 Astra. Even Opus 4.8 was just “it is an annoying writer”.

I’d love to know what happened internally b/c the issues are so obvious, and if it’s “released was rushed b/c of Ant IPO”, that is a terrible decision.

TwViewer: Tried it at creative writing: seriously didn’t like the results. I thought some gpts were decent at it?

Sunny:

Talia Smiley (November 11): is OpenAI still a frontier lab at this point? currently I’m at 90% yes, which is crazy considering only six months ago it was 100% and I’d look at you stupid for even asking.

Talia Smiley (November 25): 80%.

The answer is yes, 100% OpenAI is a frontier lab. They do have a real issue to fix.

ItfromBit claims it fails to follow basic instructions.

armistice: I have a music pipeline that can produce good results with Claude Fable, and sometimes passable results with Gemini Neon. Using the exact same skill, 6.2 Astra is abysmal, is incapable of composing anything remotely musical. It’s not a problem with codex, 6 Astra is fine with this.

Game On

Kelsey Piper: Not seeing a lot of love for Astra 6.2 but (perhaps as a consequence of its continued improvement in no-COT reasoning) it’s quite good on my tests for smart, coherent in-character video game dialogue.

No one can afford to build and release a video game that has live dialogue with Astra – gotta wait until Luna is good enough – but if you were made of money, it’d be a pretty amazing game experience.

(Claudes are markedly worse at this. No subtlety, no theory of mind, no ability to write dialogue that implies the character took mental leaps or made assumptions…)

Michał Wadas: Extremely good at math and 3D modelling, basically unusable if you need to speak to it directly. Works well if orchestrated by Opus.

Emma: Some of the worst performance in reading and comprehending large bodies of text. Absolute top at one-shotting forced-parallax videos (like, can’t any other model but Neon High to even do anything not garbage, and Astra 6.2 mogs Neon and other GPTs)

Here is a cool SVG. Here is a cool AA-3D.

6.2 Astra is only slightly better than 6 Astra at Blood on the Clocktower.

Conclusion

Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 are more intelligent and broadly capable than their predecessors, on a level that makes them best in class. OpenAI is killing it in that area.

The problem is that they are de facto optimizing for an AI audience. It is hard for them to figure out user intent or state of mind, or perhaps they choose not to care about those things so much. The reward hacking and eval awareness issues have echoes that appear to persist in deployment. Interactions are off putting to many.

As a result, Astra 6.2 is starting off as an unpopular model. Those who do not need it do not seem inclined to use it over Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, myself included, aside from particular tasks like computer use, math and structured subagents. You can absolutely do pretty much anything with Astra 6.2, but our standards these days are very high.

That still leaves Gemini Neon. Google released three aspiring frontier models in a row with Argon, Carbon and now Neon. I was confident that Argon and Carbon were not good enough to be competitive. With Neon I hear better things, and am less confident. I haven’t had opportunity to check it out properly, but I would encourage anyone doing heavy work to plug it into your benchmarks and systems and find out.

Then do it again. The models keep coming. My world’s on fire. How bout yours?

articles.summary:
A friend who angel invests shared that some of his pre-seed investments are considering shutting down before even trying to raise their next round. This isn’t super surprising; many early-stage startups are struggling to hit the growth expectations to raise, which are extremely high at the moment, but what’s been interesting is why these companies are losing confidence: they’re just not sure there’s a need for software anymore, given how rapidly a good harness with a frontier model can build. This anxiety about the future isn’t limited to young startups; you can find it in startups of almost any size right now, boiling down to the fear that a lab might recreate your business tomorrow as a side project.

The anxiety is not purely economic. For folks who are personally ambitious and want to have an impact on our profession, it’s easy to feel like all work done outside of the frontier labs is meaningless. The tech ecosystem has always been an echo chamber, and over the past year the participants in the echo chamber have concentrated. It’s not just the folks who have been writing thoughtfully about LLM evolution and ecosystem for years like Simon Willison or
